To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

c-di-GMP is a second messenger that is produced by GGDEF domain containing proteins, and degraded by EAL domain containing proteins, that is implicated in several bacterial functions such as biofilm and virulence, that is involved in cellulose synthesis and that has a role in cell division.

(1) the GGDEF domain is involved in the synthesis of c-di-Gmp, (2) the EAL domain is involved in c-di-Gmp degradation, (3) c-di-Gmp is a second messenger involved in biofilm formation and in motility, (4) c-di-GMP regulates virulence in some pathogens.
The GGDEF and Eal domains are involved in c-di-GMP synthesis and degradation respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of GGDEF and EFL domain proteins and their function in bacterial metabolism, especially in the biofilm formation process.
the identification of GGDEF and Eal domains in bacterial genomes.
the study of the role of GGDEF and EAF domains in the metabolism of bacteria, and in particular in the regulation of the production of virulence factors in the genus Salmonella.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
c-di-GMP is involved in many different processes, but it is not yet known how this is done and how it is regulated.
GGDEF and EFL domains are involved in bacterial metabolism, but the exact mechanisms are still not clear.
GGDEF proteins are involved in the synthesis of c-di-Gmp and EAL domains in its degradation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
c-di-GMP is a second messenger that regulates the cell surface properties of the bacteria.
c-di-GMP is a second messenger involved in the regulation of a wide variety of processes in bacteria.
GGDEF and EFL domains have been involved in cellulase and biofilm formation in bacteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of GGDEF and EALA domains is not restricted to a few bacterial species, but is widespread.
c-di-GMP levels are regulated by a network of proteins, including the GGDEF and EALA domains, which are able to sense environmental changes and respond accordingly.
E. coli has evolved to use a complex regulatory system involving the Eal and GGDEF domains to regulate the levels of c-di-GM P and the expression of the virulence factors.
